extracted.intended_audience: regulatory economists, agency staff, legal practitioners, and stakeholders participating in FTC rulemaking on non-compete clauses
extracted.subtask_description: Economic and compliance-cost analysis, data-selection rules, and methodological assumptions used by the FTC in its final rule on banning non‑compete clauses; intended to support regulatory impact, small-entity analysis, and responses to public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude States that broadly prohibit non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding States which broadly prohibit non-competes (CA, ND, OK, and MN) from analyses and data counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly as an inclusion/exclusion rule for patent counts, employment, and other state-level data because non-competes are not enforceable in those States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use most recent available data year
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting data series, use the most recent year with finalized estimates available (e.g., 2020 USPTO patent counts, 2019 NSF R&D spending, 2020 hospital non-profit share, 2022 BLS employment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the data source and year explicitly; note limitations when data are not broken out by State (e.g., some national R&D totals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count only granted utility patents for innovation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring patenting related to innovation, use the number of granted utility patents (patents for new or improved innovation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure comes from USPTO data and excludes States where non-competes are not enforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate regression coefficients to percent changes via exponential formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculate percent changes from estimated coefficients using the formula e^(coefficient * change) − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show use of e^(1.43*0.06)−1 and e^(2.56*0.06)−1 to translate coefficient bounds and a 0.06 enforceability decline into percent changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescale study coefficients to a 0–1 enforceability measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Rescale coefficients reported on original study scales to the Commission’s 0–1 enforceability scale when combining estimates (e.g., Starr's 0.77% corresponds to a one standard deviation; rescale by ratio of mean enforceability change to that standard deviation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rescale 0.77*(0.081/0.17)=0.364% to reflect the Commission's mean enforceability change of 0.081.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume mean magnitude change in enforceability = 0.081
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an average magnitude change in non‑compete enforceability of 0.081 (on a 0–1 scale) as the baseline multiplier in several calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This multiplier is applied when translating study coefficients to expected effects under the Commission’s estimated change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double average hourly earnings to estimate hourly output (productivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the average hourly output of workers is twice their average earnings when valuing lost productivity or output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: average earnings estimated at $30.38/hour, doubled for output valuation; Commission doubles median lawyer/HR wages similarly to reflect lost productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage rate assumption: 80% of employed individuals under Commission jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume that 80% of employed individuals are covered by the Commission's jurisdiction for counting 'covered workers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied when estimating the number of workers affected and deriving totals such as covered workers in high-use occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define high-use occupations per Starr and use BLS occupation data
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify occupations as high-use using Starr (and related work) and draw occupation-specific employment counts from BLS data (excluding CA, ND, OK, MN).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to split workers into high- and low-use occupations and to estimate counts of workers in high-use occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume certain average training quantities and firm-sponsored share
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate firm-sponsored training hours using published averages (e.g., 5.7 weeks/year * 20.1 hours/week * 73.9% firm‑sponsored = 85 hours/year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite underlying studies (Frazis & Spletzer) for the component estimates and use this to value training affected by the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume average human capital depreciation rate (20%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a human capital depreciation assumption of 20% when modeling returns to training and persistence of human capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a middle-of-the-range assumption acknowledging literature spans wide values; cite supporting literature discussing ranges from 5% to 100%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative-defaults principle (e.g., assume zero R&D effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence is uncertain or conflicting, the Commission may adopt conservative assumptions (for example, assume zero effect on R&D spending in some estimates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flagged where studies disagree or effects are statistically indistinguishable from zero; conservatism used in sensitivity/secondary calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenario analysis for hospital coverage share
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple scenarios to bound uncertainty about what share of hospitals are covered (e.g., 35% non-profits from AHA, 38.1% hospital employment at non-profits from ACS, and a 75% covered scenario).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify scenarios based on differing data sources and note that IRS tax-exempt status does not equate to Commission jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer-reviewed and working-paper coefficients with caution and note scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When importing coefficients from empirical studies (e.g., Johnson, Lipsitz, & Pei; Hausman & Lavetti; Starr; Jeffers), specify the sample, industry scope (e.g., high-technology firms), and statistical uncertainty or limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include noting when an estimate pertains only to high-technology firms or high-use industries and when covariance information is missing preventing combined uncertainty estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantified vs monetized distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify certain estimates as 'quantified but not monetized' when part of an estimate may reflect transfers rather than net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly annotate values (e.g., estimated dollar effects on earnings) as quantified but not monetized where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume firms update contractual practices with an average time estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate average firm time to change contracts (examples: a conservative 1 hour for simple cases; an average of 4–8 hours across firms; or 1.5–3 days for some firms) when estimating contract-update costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for heterogeneity: many firms may do nothing (e.g., already use NDAs, non-solicits), while others will spend multiple hours/days; justify average via examples and survey evidence on co‑use of restrictive clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume each establishment must provide its own worker notification
rubrics_metrics.description: For notice/communication cost estimates, conservatively assume each physical establishment must engage and has digital contact info for at least one worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to calculate per-establishment communication costs and to bound mailing needs (citing analogous CMS supporting statement assumptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: When commenters omit NAICS/receipts/employee counts, rely on self-description for small-business status
rubrics_metrics.description: If commenters do not provide NAICS code, annual receipts, or number of workers, the Commission will rely on the commenter’s self-description as a small business or start-up for consideration in small-entity analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note limitations and cite the SBA Table of Size Standards and Census SUSB for authoritative small-business definitions when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative federal sources for size and firm counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use SBA Table of Size Standards (13 CFR 121.201) and Census Bureau Statistics of U.S. Businesses (SUSB) for determining numbers of small firms and establishments and for firm/establishment definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values are deflated to current dollars using the BLS inflation calculator and firm/establishment definitions per Census glossary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies may redact or withhold certain public comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Posted comment counts reflect comments the agency has made publicly viewable; agencies may redact or withhold submissions (or portions) containing private/proprietary information, inappropriate language, or duplicates/near-duplicates from mass-mail campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference Regulations.gov FAQ and standard redaction/withholding practices for public comment dockets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative examples use small sample sizes for cost calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: When providing illustrative cost examples (e.g., notification costs), the Commission may choose round illustrative numbers such as 'Ten workers' and apply per-establishment average costs accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These illustrative examples are explicitly labeled and used to demonstrate method rather than serve as universal estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagging limitations when covariance or combined uncertainty cannot be estimated
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining estimates from studies, explicitly note when covariance of estimated coefficients is not reported, preventing estimation of combined uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: inability to calculate uncertainty in a combined estimate because Jeffers' study did not report covariance information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value-of-patent literature heterogeneity and caution on social value
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that literature reports highly varied estimates of the private value of patents and that the social value of a patent is understudied; present multiple estimates adjusted to current dollars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite multiple studies (Serrano, Pakes, Kogan et al.) and market reports (Richardson Oliver Insights) to show range and uncertainty in patent valuation.
